overview:
In Jain studies, “verse citations” refer to the precise, source‑grounded way of pointing to individual sutras (aphorisms), gāthās (metrical verses), or ślokas within the vast scriptural and commentarial corpus. Because Jain traditions do not revolve around a single, universally accepted “Bible,” accurate citation of verses is one of the main tools by which teachers, scholars, and lay students navigate plural canons, compare sectarian positions, and trace doctrinal lineages.

In Śvetāmbara contexts, verse citations typically refer to passages in the canonical Āgamas—Aṅgas, Upāṅgas, Prakīrṇakas, Cheda‑sūtras, Mūla‑sūtras, and Cūlikā‑sūtras—using a combination of text title, section or śrutaskandha, chapter (adhyayana), and sutra or gāthā number. For example, a citation might appear as “Ācārāṅga‑sūtra, 1.1.1” or “Sūtrakṛtāṅga 2.3.15,” indicating the hierarchical location of the verse. Later scholastic works and vernacular manuals often add further internal divisions, such as pādas (quarters of a verse) or line numbers, to make recitation and commentary easier.

In Digambara contexts, where the Śvetāmbara Āgamas are not accepted as preserved scripture, verse citations focus on other foundational works and their commentaries, such as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, Kaṣāya‑prābhṛta, and especially the Sanskrit aphoristic treatise Tattvārtha‑sūtra (also known as Mokṣa‑śāstra). Here, citations usually follow a chapter‑and‑sutra format—“Tattvārtha‑sūtra 1.1,” “5.21,” and so on—sometimes accompanied by the name of a specific commentary (e.g., Sarvārthasiddhi) when a particular interpretive tradition is being invoked. Because Tattvārtha‑sūtra is recognized as authoritative by both major sects, its verse citations often function as a shared reference point in comparative discussions.

Beyond the canons themselves, Jain verse citation practices extend to narrative, ethical, and cosmological literature in Prakrit, Sanskrit, and modern languages. Commentators frequently quote earlier verses verbatim, then gloss them word by word, creating chains of citation that link doctrinal claims to earlier authorities. Modern scholarly works and community education materials usually preserve traditional numbering while adding standardized transliteration and translation, so that a single verse can be reliably located across different editions and languages.

Technically, verse citations serve several functions. They anchor doctrinal statements in identifiable textual loci; they allow cross‑checking between manuscripts and printed editions; they make visible where sectarian or regional recensions diverge in verse counts or wording; and they help distinguish between primary scripture (āgama or siddhānta), classical commentary (ṭīkā, vṛtti), and later didactic literature. In practice, this means that responsible Jain teaching and academic work will not simply paraphrase ideas, but will indicate the exact verse or sutra from which a claim is drawn, often noting when numbering differs between Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions or between major editions.

Because transmission has occurred over centuries of oral recitation, manuscript copying, and regional redaction, verse citation is also tied to questions of textual criticism and authority. Some works survive only in partial form; others have variant verse orders or counts; still others are known through quotations in later commentaries. Careful citation therefore includes awareness of which edition or recension is being used, and it may flag places where the verse numbering in a modern printed text does not match older catalogues or sectarian lists. In contemporary Jain studies, this attention to verse citations is essential for distinguishing direct quotation from paraphrase, for mapping doctrinal development, and for maintaining intellectual honesty about the limits of our evidence.

For lay practice, verse citations appear in prayer books, daily recitation guides, and ethical handbooks, where key verses—such as those on the Three Jewels (ratna‑traya), vows (vrata), or non‑violence (ahiṃsā)—are singled out with clear references so that they can be memorized, recited, and discussed. Youth and family education often introduces students to the idea that every familiar verse has a textual home, and that learning to read citations is part of entering the wider world of Jain scripture and philosophy. In this way, verse citation is not merely a technical scholarly tool, but a living practice that connects contemporary Jains to the remembered words of teachers and the evolving interpretive traditions that surround them.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra 1.1
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāti (Umāsvāmi)
primary_sources.translation: Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct are the path to liberation.
primary_sources.notes: This opening verse of Tattvārtha-sūtra is one of the most frequently cited Jain scriptural passages, used across Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions. In citation practice it is usually referenced as “TS 1.1” or “Tattvārtha-sūtra, chapter 1, sutra 1.” Commentaries such as Pūjyapāda’s Sarvārthasiddhi quote the verse verbatim and then unpack each term—samyag-darśana, jñāna, cāritra—in detail, illustrating how verse citation anchors doctrinal exposition. Modern translations and study guides preserve the chapter-and-sutra numbering so that readers can correlate the English rendering with the Sanskrit original and with traditional commentarial literature.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga-sūtra (Śvetāmbara canon)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the disciples of Mahāvīra; exact authorship not individually named
primary_sources.original_text: जे ण हन्ति ण घातेति, ण च हन्तव्वं समुप्पादेति, ण च अनुमोदेति, ण च तस्स कारणं कुंति, ण च तस्स निमित्तं होति, ण च तस्स उपकारं कुंति, ण च तस्स साहायं कुंति, ण च तस्स संनिव्वत्तिं कुंति, ण च तस्स संनिव्वत्तिमुप्पादेति—सो खु अहिंसको ति वुच्चइ.
primary_sources.transliteration: je ṇ hanti ṇ ghāteti, ṇ ca hantavvaṃ samuppādeti, ṇ ca anumodeti, ṇ ca tassa kāraṇaṃ kuṃti, ṇ ca tassa nimittaṃ hoti, ṇ ca tassa upakāraṃ kuṃti, ṇ ca tassa sāhāyaṃ kuṃti, ṇ ca tassa saṃnivvattaṃ kuṃti, ṇ ca tassa saṃnivvattimuppādeti—so khu ahiṃsako ti vuccai.
primary_sources.translation: One who does not kill, does not cause killing, does not approve of killing, does not provide the cause, does not become the occasion, does not render assistance, does not support, does not bring about the cessation of life, and does not instigate such cessation—such a person is called non-violent.
primary_sources.notes: This well-known Prakrit passage on non-violence is cited from the Ācārāṅga-sūtra, typically referenced with a hierarchical citation such as “Ācārāṅga 1.1.4” or similar, depending on the edition and internal division into śrutaskandhas and adhyayanas. Traditional and modern commentaries quote the verse to define ahiṃsā in detail, and responsible citation practice notes the exact location in the canon, sometimes with variant numbering across different Śvetāmbara recensions. The example illustrates how a single verse becomes a doctrinal touchstone, repeatedly cited in ethical discussions and educational materials.

misconceptions.myth: Verse citations are purely a modern academic convention and were not important in traditional Jain practice.
misconceptions.reality: While modern scholarship has standardized many citation formats, the careful identification of verses by text, section, and internal numbering has long been integral to Jain monastic and scholastic traditions. Recitation lineages, commentaries, and doctrinal debates all rely on knowing exactly where a verse occurs, and traditional catalogues and mnemonic diagrams already encode verse counts and divisions.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain communities use the same verse numbering and canon, so citations are automatically uniform across sects.
misconceptions.reality: Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions differ in which texts they recognize as preserved scripture, and even within a single tradition, manuscripts and printed editions can vary in verse counts and internal divisions. Responsible citation therefore includes awareness of sectarian context and edition, and may note when numbering differs or when a verse is known only through later quotation.

misconceptions.myth: A paraphrased teaching is equivalent to a verse citation and does not need a precise reference.
misconceptions.reality: Paraphrase can be useful for explanation, but it does not replace the need to identify the exact verse or sutra from which a teaching is drawn. Precise citation allows others to verify wording, examine context, and see how commentaries interpret the passage. In Jain studies, distinguishing between direct quotation, paraphrase, and interpretive expansion is a core part of honest engagement with scripture.

misconceptions.myth: Because Tattvārtha-sūtra is accepted by both major sects, its verses can be cited without mentioning chapter and sutra numbers.
misconceptions.reality: The cross-sectarian authority of Tattvārtha-sūtra makes precise citation even more important. Indicating chapter and sutra numbers—such as “TS 1.1” or “5.21”—allows readers from different traditions and language backgrounds to locate the same passage, compare translations, and consult their own commentarial lineages. Omitting such details weakens the shared reference point that the text provides.
